title: Collective nouns
subtitle: a flock of sheep, a bunch of flowers
summary: Learn the nouns English uses for groups - of people, animals, landscape features and everyday things - and whether they take a singular or a plural verb.

lesson.heading: Groups of people
lesson.text: Collective nouns describe a group of the same people or things. For people in general, **a group** suggests a smaller number and **a crowd** a large one. **A gang** is rather negative.

examples.text: A small **group of people** was waiting outside the office.
There was a huge **crowd of people** at the concert.
There was a **gang of youths** on the corner; they didn't look very friendly.
The police are looking for a **gang of thieves**.

lesson.heading: Words used with particular animals
rows: sheep, or birds such as geese and pigeons
fish - a shoal of herring / mackerel
insects, typically flying ones - a swarm of bees / gnats / mosquitoes
dogs, hyenas, wolves - and also playing cards
lesson.note: Note the singular form of the fish name after shoal: a shoal of herring, not ~~herrings~~.

lesson.heading: People doing the same job
lesson.text: These collective nouns take a **singular or a plural verb**, depending on whether you are thinking of the group as one body or as separate individuals. Staff is normally used with a plural verb.

examples.text: A **team** of rescue workers was / were at the scene of the disaster.
The **crew** was / were saved when the ship sank.
examples.note: crew = the workers on a ship, ambulance or plane

examples.text: The **company** is / are rehearsing a new production.

examples.note: cast = the actors in a film or play
staff = any group who share a place of work

lesson.note: The public also takes either verb: The public has / have a right to know the truth.

lesson.heading: Landscape and everyday things
rows: two things that are the same - a pair of birds
a vague way of saying two - a couple of strawberries
papers, clothes, dishes, toys, bed linen
tools, pots and pans, dishes, glasses

left.label: a pair of
left.text: Two of anything that are **the same**.
examples: There was a **pair of birds** sitting on a branch.
She gave me a **pair of silver candlesticks**.

right.label: a couple of
right.text: A vague way of saying two - they are **not necessarily identical**.
examples: Could you put a **couple of spoons of sugar** in this coffee?
I'll be back in a **couple of minutes**.

lesson.heading: Collective nouns for language
lesson.text: Some collective nouns are used with words about speaking and writing. They are common in journalism and in formal writing.

examples.text: The journalists raised a **host of** difficult questions.
examples.note: a host of = a large number of

examples.text: There had been a **barrage of** complaints about police violence.
examples.note: a barrage of = a rapid, aggressive stream of

examples.text: He was not prepared to listen to a **string of** wild accusations.
He just gave a **series of** short answers that left everyone dissatisfied.

lesson.text: If you cannot remember the special word, *a group of* is almost always safe - but the specific one, like *a shoal of fish*, sounds far more natural.

exercises.prompt: Match each collective noun with the word that follows it.
As we looked into the water, we saw a ___ of brightly coloured fish.
exercises.hint: (the word for a group of fish)
exercises.explanation: Fish move in a shoal; insects in a swarm.

exercises.prompt: There's a ___ of cards on the bookshelf. Will you fetch them for me, please?
exercises.explanation: A pack of cards, and also a pack of dogs or wolves.

exercises.prompt: A ___ of biologists is studying marine life in this area.
exercises.explanation: Team takes a singular or a plural verb, depending on your point of view.

exercises.prompt: Look at that ___ of birds on that tree. Both of them have beautiful markings.
exercises.explanation: A pair is two of anything that are the same.

exercises.prompt: Could you put a ___ of spoons of sugar in this coffee for me? Yes, just two, that's fine.
exercises.explanation: A couple of is an approximate two; a pair of is two matching things.

exercises.prompt: Which word does NOT go with *company*?
exercises.explanation: A company is a group of performers, not of swimmers.

exercises.prompt: Which word does NOT go with *crew*?
exercises.explanation: A hospital has staff; a ship, plane or ambulance has a crew.

exercises.prompt: Which word does NOT go with *flock*?
exercises.explanation: Flock is for sheep and birds. Pigs are kept in a herd.

exercises.prompt: Which collective noun goes with each animal?

exercises.statement: There is a stack of tables in the next room.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a stack is things placed on top of one another: chairs, tables, boxes, logs.

exercises.statement: A herd of sheep had escaped from a field.
exercises.explanation: A flock of sheep had escaped from a field. Herd is for cows, deer and goats.

exercises.answer: She gave me a bunch of beautiful roses for my birthday.
alternatives: She gave me a beautiful bunch of roses for my birthday.
exercises.explanation: Bunch goes with flowers, grapes and bananas.
